newsitem.title: UK: Mark firmer in Europe as market mulls EMI report.
newsitem.headline: Mark firmer in Europe as market mulls EMI report.

text.p: The mark was firmer on its European crosses on Tuesday as the market digested the European Monetary Institute's (EMI) annual report.

The EMI, forerunner of the European central bank, expressed serious concerns that many European Union states have not yet managed to rein in their national deficits enough to launch the single currency in 1999.
This comes after six leading economic institutes on Sunday said Germany would miss the European Monetary Union (EMU) three percent budget deficit target.
The EMI report threw some cold water on the renewed EMU enthusiasm but analysts said it was unlikely to reverse sentiment entirely.

"Anything that suggests the German budget deficit is overshooting will be perceived by the markets as increasing the likelihood of a broad-based EMU," Bank America chief economist Jeremy Hawkins said. "It's also providing a weak mark on the increasing perception of a soft euro," he added.
The Swedish crown dropped in early trade after Swedish media published a customary leaked budget showing the government had doubled its forecast extra spending to 20 billion crowns.
Prime Minister Goran Persson's government in January announced it would spend 10 billion crowns on social measures in a bid to halve unemployment by the year 2000.
The budget is due to be announced at 1100 GMT.
Mark/crown was trading at 4.4420/40 by 0844 GMT, compared with 4.4295/25 late in Europe on Monday.

The lira continued to bounce off support around 982, but would find it difficult to continue appreciating given Italy's weak GDP data yesterday and this morning's industrial production numbers, BZW currency strategist Chris Turner said.
"We remain sceptical about Italy's ability to qualify for EMU," he added.
Italian industrial production fell 3.8 percent year-on-year in February against forecasts for a 2.3 percent drop.
Mark/lira was trading at 983.40/3.70 against 983.35/85 on Monday.
The peseta was trading at 84.21/23 from 84.14 at the previous close after a widely-expected key money market rate cut by the Bank of Spain to 5.50 percent from 5.75 percent.
The rate cut comes after benign March inflation data, released last week, which showed inflation dropping to 2.2 percent, the lowest level in nearly 30 years.
Dealers said the rate cut was likely to lend support to the peseta but that the Spanish unit was under profit-taking pressure after its rise to 10-week highs at 84.08 on Monday.
